title: The twelve (Mark 3:1–19)
hook: a withered hand healed, then he names twelve to be with him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabbath, made for people. Your line was rest is for you. Did you take a real rest, without apologizing? Today, one more sabbath, and then a list of names. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Think of any team you've been picked for. A class project, a work crew, a band, a game in the park. You probably assume you were picked for what you could do. Your speed, your skills, your ideas. In today's reading Jesus climbs a hill, calls the people he wants, and chooses twelve. Mark lists them by name. And before he says anything about what they'll do, he says why he chose them, and it's not what you'd expect. Today's word is what they were called: apostle.
screen: `PICKED FOR A TEAM.` → `TWELVE CALLED UP A HILL.` → `CHOSEN FOR WHAT?`

segments.voice: First, a hand. It starts on another sabbath, in a synagogue, with a man whose hand is withered. People watch to see what Jesus will do. He asks them, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy?" Nobody answers. Mark says Jesus looked round at them with anger, grieved at the hardness of their hearts. Then he says to the man: stretch forth thy hand. And it's restored. Second, the hill. After this, Jesus goes up a mountain and calls those he wants, and they come. And Mark says: "And he made that twelve should be with him, and that he might send them to preach." Twelve is no accident. Israel had twelve tribes; Jesus is gathering a people. Third, the order. Read it again. First, to be with him. Then, to be sent. Before any preaching or healing, the job is to be with him: walk the roads, eat at the same fire, watch him pray at dawn. Fourth, the names. Simon, whom he names Peter. James and John, whom he nicknames sons of thunder. Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddeus, Simon the Cananean, and Judas Iscariot, who, Mark tells us right away, would betray him. Fishermen, a tax collector, and a hothead or two. Apostle is Greek, apostolos, one who is sent. Catholics believe the bishops today are the apostles' successors, a line that runs, they say, all the way back to that hill.
screen: `STRETCH FORTH THY HAND.` · `TWELVE, LIKE THE TWELVE TRIBES.` · `FIRST WITH HIM, THEN SENT.` · `FISHERMEN, A TAX MAN, A BETRAYER.` · then, large: `THAT TWELVE SHOULD BE WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: your twelve. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you really walk through life with, the ones you'd call at two in the morning, the ones who've watched you at your worst. Let their names come one at a time. You may not get to twelve. That's fine. If you can, write them down. If you pray, you can hold each name before God for a moment. If you don't, just be grateful, one name at a time. The bell holds the time.
Apostle. From the Greek apostolos, one who is sent. But in Mark, the twelve are called first to be with him. Today's word.
Your line: first, to be with him. Today, with someone you love, don't try to do anything for them for ten minutes. Just be with them. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics keep feast days for each of the apostles through the year, and profess in the Creed that the Church is apostolic, led by bishops understood as the apostles' successors.

what it means: one who is sent, but in Mark, called first to be with Jesus.
what a scholar hears: apostolos, from apostellō, to send; twelve as a sign of Israel's twelve tribes regathered.
